## 📅 General info about the deadline

> ⚠️ **IMPORTANT DEADLINE**: 2026-10-21 20:00 (Vilnius time)

- Maximum points if completed by the deadline: **1.5**
- Late submission: **20%** reduction of the maximum mark for each week late.
- Minimum expectation: **at least 75%** of the requirements implemented - quality of implementation matters, not just presence.
- Covers material from lectures 1-6.

## 🎤 Presentation

- You prepared an actual presentation: a **working app demo** (slides are optional, but a running application is not) and you are ready to present it to the other teams.
- Every team member can present the tasks they did. Expect that every member will be asked to talk during or after the presentation.
- You can show every implemented requirement **in your code**, not just in the running app.
- I may pick a requirement and a random team member and ask them to find it in the code, explain it, and make a small change on-site.

## ⭐ Goals

### 🎯 Official goal

Develop a **web** application using the material covered in lectures 1-6:

- You have a **working** (alpha) version of your app, and at least one user scenario can be demonstrated end to end.
- The app has a functional UI (front-end), an API (back-end), and the front-end makes meaningful calls to the API.
- You worked as a team and can prove it: commits, pull requests, reviews, working app.
- **Every** team member knows and understands the material from lectures 1-6.

### 🎯 Additional (unofficial) goal

Understand how to use GitHub and code as a team, prepare a foundation for future work, learn to review your own code and to take feedback when you get it.

## ✅ Requirements

Each requirement below has three parts:

- **What we check** - what must exist in your code.
- **👥 Every team member** - what each person must be able to explain or write on-site.
- **Good vs bad** - a short example. Each has a **Read more** link to a separate page with more examples and explanations.

> 💡 The word **meaningfully** is on purpose. A feature used only to tick the box (a wrapper that adds nothing, a struct that should be a class) does not count.

---

### ⚙️ 1. The application can be interacted with using *some* sort of interface

**What we check**

- The application has a user interface (it is not just an API or a console app).
- The interface is interactive: the user presses elements and gets results.
- There is at least one user scenario that can be demonstrated **end to end** (UI → API → result shown back in the UI).

**👥 Every team member** can show the scenario and say which parts of the code it touches.

**Good vs bad**

```csharp
// ✅ GOOD: the UI's "RSVP" button calls the API, the API changes data, the UI shows the new state.
// POST /api/studysessions/5/rsvp  ->  204 No Content  ->  UI re-fetches and shows "4 seats left"

// ❌ BAD: a page that only displays hard-coded data and a button that does nothing.
// <button onClick={() => {}}>RSVP</button>
```

📖 [Read more](examples/01-user-interface.md)

---

### ⚙️ 2. Your own `class`, `struct`, `record` and `enum` (one type must be immutable)

**What we check**

- At least one **meaningfully** used class, struct, record and enum of your own.
- At least one of your types is **immutable**.

**👥 Every team member** can point to each of these in the code and explain why it is that kind of type; knows the differences between class, struct and record; knows what an enum is and what an enum with `[Flags]` is.

**Good vs bad**

```csharp
// ✅ GOOD: an immutable record - a read-only projection with value equality, no identity.
public record StudySessionSummary(string Course, string Topic, DateTimeOffset StartsAt, int SeatsAvailable);

// ✅ GOOD: an enum replaces "magic" numbers scattered across the code.
public enum SessionStatus { Scheduled, Full }

// ❌ BAD: a struct with a lot of data and mutable fields - it should be a class.
public struct StudySession { public int Id; public string Topic; public string Notes; /* ... */ }
```

📖 [Read more](examples/02-class-struct-record-enum.md)

---

### ⚙️ 3. Property usage in `struct` and `class`

**What we check**

- At least one **meaningfully** used property in a class and in a struct.

**👥 Every team member** can point to properties and explain them; knows all kinds (normal property, auto-implemented property, indexer) and can write them on-site.

**Good vs bad**

```csharp
// ✅ GOOD: validation on the way in, a computed property on the way out.
public SessionStatus Status => SeatsAvailable > 0 ? SessionStatus.Scheduled : SessionStatus.Full;

// ❌ BAD: a property that is just a public field wearing a costume,
// next to a hand-written Get/Set method pair that should have been a property.
private string _topic;
public string GetTopic() => _topic;
public void SetTopic(string value) => _topic = value;
```

📖 [Read more](examples/03-properties.md)

---

### ⚙️ 4. Named and optional arguments

**What we check**

- At least one **meaningfully** used named argument and at least one **meaningfully** used optional argument.

**👥 Every team member** can point to them, explain why they are there, and write them on-site.

**Good vs bad**

```csharp
// ✅ GOOD: asOf is optional (defaults to "now"); naming skips the first optional parameter.
sessions.UpcomingOnly(asOf: someDate);
sessions.Filter(minSeatsAvailable: 2);

// ❌ BAD: optional parameters used to avoid thinking, and named arguments on a one-parameter call.
void Save(string a = "", string b = "", string c = "", bool d = false, bool e = true) { }
Save(a: "x");
```

📖 [Read more](examples/04-named-optional-arguments.md)

---

### ⚙️ 5. Extension methods

**What we check**

- At least one **meaningfully** used extension method.

**👥 Every team member** can point to it, explain why it is an extension method, and write one on-site.

**Good vs bad**

```csharp
// ✅ GOOD: extends a type you do not own (IEnumerable<T>) with domain behavior.
public static IEnumerable<StudySession> UpcomingOnly(this IEnumerable<StudySession> sessions, DateTimeOffset? asOf = null)
    => sessions.Where(s => s.StartsAt > (asOf ?? DateTimeOffset.UtcNow));

// ❌ BAD: an extension on your own class - you own it, so just add a method to it.
public static void PrintInfo(this StudySession session) => Console.WriteLine(session.Topic);
```

📖 [Read more](examples/05-extension-methods.md)

### ⚙️ 6. Iterating through collections the right way

**What we check**

- At least one **meaningfully** used iteration through a collection, using the recommended constructs.

**👥 Every team member** can point to it and explain why that kind of loop (or LINQ) was chosen.

**Good vs bad**

```csharp
// ✅ GOOD: foreach when you only read; no index needed.
foreach (var session in sessions)
{
    Console.WriteLine(session.Topic);
}

// ❌ BAD: modifying a collection while iterating it (throws InvalidOperationException).
foreach (var session in sessions)
{
    if (session.SeatsAvailable == 0) sessions.Remove(session);
}
```

📖 [Read more](examples/06-collection-iteration.md)

### ⚙️ 7. Using a stream to load data

**What we check**

- At least one **meaningfully** used stream reading operation (file, web response, socket...).
- The stream is wrapped in a `using` statement/declaration.

**👥 Every team member** can point to it, and knows streams, stream readers and `using`.

**Good vs bad**

```csharp
// ✅ GOOD: read line by line, disposed automatically, not blocking a thread.
await using var stream = File.OpenRead("sessions.csv");
using var reader = new StreamReader(stream);
while (await reader.ReadLineAsync() is { } line)
{
    // parse line
}

// ❌ BAD: never disposed - the file stays locked until the garbage collector gets to it.
var reader = new StreamReader("sessions.csv");
var text = reader.ReadToEnd();
```

📖 [Read more](examples/07-streams.md)

---

### ⚙️ 8. LINQ to Objects (methods or query syntax)

**What we check**

- At least one **meaningfully** used LINQ to Objects query.
- Where LINQ is *not* used in a scenario where it fits, you can justify it.

**👥 Every team member** can point to it and write a query on-site, in both method syntax and query syntax.

> 📝 LINQ to Entities (queries against a database through Entity Framework) is **not** LINQ to Objects. LINQ to Objects queries in-memory collections.

**Good vs bad**

```csharp
// ✅ GOOD: filter, project, order - one readable pipeline.
var topics = sessions
    .Where(s => s.SeatsAvailable > 0)
    .OrderBy(s => s.StartsAt)
    .Select(s => s.Topic)
    .ToList();

// ❌ BAD: a query that rebuilds what a property already gives you.
var count = sessions.Select(s => s).Where(s => true).ToList().Count();
```

📖 [Read more](examples/08-linq-to-objects.md)

---

### ⚙️ 9. At least one standard .NET interface

(`IEnumerable`, `IComparable`, `IComparer`, `IEquatable`, `IEnumerator`, etc.)

**What we check**

- At least one **meaningfully** implemented standard .NET interface.

**👥 Every team member** can point to it and knows what `IComparable`/`IComparer`/`IEquatable` and `IEnumerable`/`IEnumerator` are for.

**Good vs bad**

```csharp
// ✅ GOOD: the type defines its own natural ordering, so List<T>.Sort() just works.
public class StudySession : IComparable<StudySession>
{
    public int CompareTo(StudySession? other) => other is null ? 1 : StartsAt.CompareTo(other.StartsAt);
}

// ❌ BAD: implements the interface to satisfy the checklist, then throws.
public int CompareTo(StudySession? other) => throw new NotImplementedException();
```

📖 [Read more](examples/09-standard-interfaces.md)

### ⚙️ 10. Pull requests and reviews

**What we check**

- **All** changes reach `main` through pull requests, with no direct pushes.
- Every PR has a description explaining **what** was done and **why**.
- **Every** team member authored at least **3 merged PRs** and reviewed at least **3** PRs of teammates.
- A PR counts as reviewed only with **meaningful** comments and discussion - "LGTM" alone does not count, and at least some comments should lead to changes.

**👥 Every team member** can open any of their PRs and explain it.

**Good vs bad**

```text
✅ GOOD review comment:  "Filter() is called twice per request here - can we call it once and reuse the result? Line 42."
❌ BAD review comment:   "looks good"
```

📖 [Read more](examples/10-pull-requests-and-reviews.md)

---

### ⚙️ 11. Uniform coding style

**What we check**

- One consistent coding style across the whole project (formatting, naming, file layout).
- It is enforced by tooling, not by hoping: `.editorconfig`, `dotnet format`, a formatter on the front-end.

**👥 Every team member** knows how to apply the formatter and where the team's rules are written down.

**Good vs bad**

```csharp
// ✅ GOOD: PascalCase members, camelCase locals, one brace style - everywhere.
public int SeatsAvailable { get; set; }

// ❌ BAD: three styles in one file because three people wrote it.
public int seats_available { get; set; }
public string  Topic{get;set;}
```

📖 [Read more](examples/11-coding-style.md)
